newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Ruined Albanians latest victims of pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Ruined Albanians latest victims of pyramid schemes.

text.p: Albanians protesting after being pushed to the brink of ruin were the latest victims of dubious pyramid schemes collapsing throughout eastern Europe after luring investors with promises of high and quick returns.
This week's violence in the southern town of Vlore, in which three people have died, and five days of peaceful marches which preceded it, was sparked by one of five such failures.

Albanians proved easy prey for fast-talking financiers as the poorest people in ex-communist eastern Europe and the least exposed to market economics after four decades of harsh isolation and repression under Stalinist strongman Enver Hoxha.
Gullible investors were initially promised monthly interest of 20 percent, with some rates rising last year to 200 percent per quarter -- in effect tripling their stakes within three months.

Pyramid schemes flourish "mathematically" in a post-communist legal void, by paying interest to older investors with deposits taken from the new. The system collapses when it runs out of new customers.

That was the fate Russia's MMM scheme, which went down with $1 billion in depositors' money in 1994, and Caritas in Romania, which sank with similar debts after offering investors eight times their stake within three months.
But unlike those schemes, which burned out within 18 months, Albania's versions proved more durable, holding out for most of the six years since the collapse of communism.
That generated allegations, never proven, that much of the money circulating through them originated from criminal activity abroad.
Experts say money coming in from Albanians working abroad has been another key source of funds. Remittances from abroad were officially estimated at around $400 million in 1995.
Economists say a total of up to $2 billion may have been sunk in the schemes. Albania's gross domestic product stood at little over $2.5 billion at the end of last year.

Opposition politicians accuse President Sali Berisha of doing nothing to check the spread of the funds. Some even say his Democratic Party used proceeds from them to finance his re-election campaign last year.
Alarm bells were first set off in mid-January when a fund operated by "Sude", a 32-year-old Gypsy woman, folded with debts of $100 million to her 100,000 depositors.
Up to 2,000 depositors had queued outside her office daily from dawn until midnight before the crash. Sude is now in jail.
Two other firms, Xhaferri and Populli, styled themselves as charities and promised investors they could triple deposits every three months over two years.
Offices were set up in Albania's remote, backward villages, prompting farmers to sell cattle and land.

Acting under pressure from the International Monetary Fund to crack down on the schemes, the government last month froze $300 million amassed by the two funds in state banks. Investors are now getting back 50 to 60 percent of their stakes.

The Gjallica fund, based in Vlore, was the last straw for people in more volatile southern Albania who, virtually to a man, had poured their life savings into the plan. Depositors are owed about $500 million with no sign yet of refunds, leaving thousands of investors destitute and angry.
The biggest questions now centre on Vefa holdings, by far the country's largest company with interests in supermarkets, hotels, petrol stations and breweries.
Newspapers increasingly aggressive towards Berisha's government suggest it is only a matter of time before Vefa collapses, an allegation Vefa managers vigorously reject.
Vefa has cut monthly interest payments to three percent, and investors cannot draw on their capital.
